cur:catacombs-maius-good-shepherd-ceilin.summary: A cross-vault is divided into painted fields: at the centre the Good Shepherd carries a sheep, surrounded by Jonah resting under his vine, Adam and Eve, a praying orans and decorative motifs. The programme gathers images of salvation around Christ the Shepherd, who stands in the very centre of the ceiling above the dead.
facts: According to the Commons description of Wilpert's plate 171, the centre shows the Good Shepherd, the right Jonah in repose, the left Adam and Eve, and the bottom an orans.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.
cur:catacombs-maius-good-shepherd-ceilin.notes: As elsewhere, the Good Shepherd is read as a symbol of Christ in this Christian context.

cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-ab.summary: Carved in a yellowish stone, the frieze unfolds in three groups. At the left, the hand of God stays Abraham's knife as he holds Isaac; in the centre a bearded Christ stands on the mountain of Paradise between palm trees, handing a scroll to Peter while Paul acclaims him; at the right a youthful, long-haired Christ touches the eyes of a blind man with his finger. The gable-roofed lid imitates the tiles of a house, a home for the dead.
facts: It was found in 1970 during work to strengthen a pillar of the nave and had never been opened.
The burial was a woman of about twenty, dressed in silk with gold-thread bands, wearing a crown of plants and a gold cross on her forehead, and laid with incense.
Analysis of the skeleton showed after-effects of poliomyelitis in the right leg.
cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-ab.notes: Robert Valette's Commons description dates it to the mid-5th century.

cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-lamb-sea-o.summary: Beneath a heading naming the seven angels with the last plagues, seven winged angels holding vials stand in the upper register; a band of interlace separates them from the lower scene, where the Lamb with a cross-staff stands at the centre between the saints, who play harps and raise them in praise above a dark sea of glass.
facts: The Morgan Beatus is the work of the painter-scribe Magius (Maius), who is named in a colophon on fol. 293; it is one of the earliest works of the revived Spanish Apocalypse tradition and of so-called Mozarabic art.
The manuscript has 300 leaves of fine parchment and contains, besides Beatus's Commentary, Jerome's Commentary on Daniel.
cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-lamb-sea-o.notes: Christ appears as the Lamb. Folio not stated on the Commons file.

cur:objects-monza-ampulla-adoration.summary: The face of this pilgrim's flask shows the Virgin enthroned frontally with the Christ Child on her lap, with the star above; the Magi approach from one side bearing gifts and the shepherds with their flocks from the other. A Greek inscription runs around the rim. Brought back from the Holy Land filled with oil from the holy places, such flasks carried images of the Gospel events that had taken place there.
facts: Wikipedia describes the Monza ampullae as the largest collection of Early Medieval pilgrimage flasks for holy oil from the Holy Land, made in Palestine probably in the 5th to early 7th centuries and kept in Monza Cathedral since they were donated by Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards (c. 570–628).
They were mass-produced souvenirs, filled with oil from lamps burning before the holy shrines, and their images played a crucial part in establishing the iconography of many Christian subjects.
cur:objects-monza-ampulla-adoration.notes: The only freely licensed image found is a historic glass lantern slide (University of Leuven) reproducing an engraving of the ampulla, not a photograph of the object. The specific ampulla number in Monza could not be identified.

met:460946.summary: In this gilt-bronze pax, the Virgin sits enthroned before a backdrop of classical arches and buildings, tenderly drawing the Christ Child to her cheek while the young Saint John the Baptist, haloed, leans against her knee. Her mantle falls in rich patterned folds, and the whole is enclosed in an elaborate scrolled frame with cherub heads. A pax was offered to the faithful to kiss during Mass as the sign of peace, so this intimate image of the Holy Family was made to be touched in devotion.
facts: The Met dates the model to the third quarter and this cast to the last quarter of the 16th century, probably Rome.
The frame was cast in four separate parts and riveted at each corner; the reverse has a reddish-brown patina while the face is gilt.
It belongs to the Robert Lehman Collection, given to the Met in 1975.
met:460946.notes: Worklist year 900 was an error: this is a late Renaissance work (late 16th century). It depicts the Christ Child, so it remains in the collection, but belongs with 16th-century works.

walters:41.325.summary: At the right end of this marble fragment a youthful shepherd with thick curls carries a lamb across his shoulders, holding its legs, while two sheep look up at him from below. The rest of the surface is filled with the S-shaped fluting (strigilation) typical of Roman sarcophagi. According to the Walters, the fragment comes from a small Early Christian sarcophagus probably made for a child, for whom the image of Christ the Good Shepherd carrying his sheep home was a fitting consolation.
facts: The Walters dates the fragment to the early 4th century (300–325) and describes the sarcophagus as probably made for a child.
The museum notes that the Good Shepherd image grew out of the pagan figure of Hermes as ram-bearer before it was taken up as an image of Jesus.
It entered the Walters in 2001, purchased from Royal-Athena Galleries.

walters:71.272.summary: Under rows of five trefoil arches, this large Gothic diptych unfolds the story of salvation in three tiers. Reading from the top left come the Annunciation, the Nativity and the Adoration of the Magi; then the Kiss of Judas with the Death of Judas, the Crucifixion and the Resurrection; and finally the Ascension and Pentecost. Densely peopled yet clearly ordered, it offered its owner the whole Gospel in a single opening.
walters:71.272.scripture: Luke 1:26–38; Luke 2:1–20; Matthew 2:1–12; Matthew 26:47–50; Matthew 27:3–5; John 19:16–37; Matthew 28:1–10; Acts 1:9–11; Acts 2:1–4
facts: The diptych once had a stand, attached through square holes in the centre arch of the lower arcades (now plugged with ivory); the outline of the stand is incised on the back.
The Walters cites it as the model for the smaller Nativity and Adoration diptych 71.194.
It belonged to John Malcolm of Poltalloch, was exhibited at Manchester (1857) and Leeds (1868), and was sold in London in 1913.
walters:71.272.notes: Worklist year 850 was a parsing error for '4th quarter 14th century'.

Q110487317.summary: Kneeling beside a rock in the night garden, Christ lifts his face toward a shaft of heavenly light, his hands clasped in surrender as the disciples sleep in the shadows behind him. Heinrich Hofmann's tender, devotional image became one of the most widely reproduced pictures of Jesus in the 20th century, printed in Bibles, Sunday-school materials and church bulletins worldwide.
facts: Hofmann, a professor at the Dresden Academy, specialized in scenes from the life of Christ; his Christ in the Temple hangs in Dresden's Gemäldegalerie.
John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought it together with Hofmann's Christ and the Rich Young Ruler and a studio version of Christ in the Temple; all three are now at Riverside Church in New York.
According to Riverside Church, Christ in Gethsemane is one of the most copied paintings in the world.
The subject is Christ's prayer in the garden: "not my will, but thine, be done."
